hypotheses.title: GTC transferFrom bypasses allowance check enabling arbitrary token theft in tests
hypotheses.description: transferFrom explicitly removed the allowance check ("Removed allowance check for easy testing") and transfers tokens from any src to any dst without verifying msg.sender has approval. Any external caller can drain any account's balance to any destination. Even though the file header says "not audited," the contest scope includes it and the lens includes replay/signature-adjacent authorization issues. This is a straightforward unauthorized-transfer primitive reachable by any untrusted actor.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls transferFrom(victim, attacker, victimBalance). 2) Contract executes _transferTokens without allowance check. 3) Victim's GTC tokens are moved to attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of funds from any holder's balance; arbitrary token theft.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restore the allowance check (or mark this file strictly out of scope in writing).

hypotheses.title: transferFrom in GTC mock has allowance check removed
hypotheses.description: The `transferFrom` function explicitly removed the allowance check ("Removed allowance check for easy testing"), so any caller can move tokens from any `src` address to any `dst` address without approval. Although the file is marked as a test mock, it is included in the in-scope file list and is used as the staking token in tests; if this mock is ever deployed or reused, it allows arbitrary theft of balances.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `transferFrom(victim, attacker, victimBalance)`. 2) No allowance is checked, so `_transferTokens` moves the full balance to the attacker. 3) Attacker repeats for all holders.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of all token balances for every holder; total insolvency of the token.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restore the allowance check (`allowances[src][msg.sender]`) and decrement it, or clearly exclude this file from scope and never deploy it.

hypotheses.title: release() can restore slashed funds without re-crediting userTotalStaked
hypotheses.description: When a slash occurs, `userTotalStaked[staker]` is decremented by `slashedAmount`. When `release()` restores funds, it increments `selfStakes[staker].amount` (or `communityStakes[staker][stakee].amount`) but never increments `userTotalStaked[staker]`. This causes `userTotalStaked` to permanently under-report the staker's actual stake, breaking any downstream accounting that relies on it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes 100 GTC via `selfStake`; `userTotalStaked = 100`. 2) Slasher slashes 50%; `amount = 50`, `slashedAmount = 50`, `userTotalStaked = 50`. 3) Releaser calls `release(staker, staker, 50, round)`; `amount` becomes 100 again, but `userTotalStaked` stays at 50. 4) Attacker now has 100 GTC staked but `userTotalStaked` reports 50. Any logic (or external integrator) using `userTotalStaked` for voting weight, eligibility, or further slashing math is now wrong.
hypotheses.impact: Persistent accounting drift between `userTotalStaked` and actual stake balances. Downstream consumers (governance, eligibility, future slashing) operate on incorrect totals; the staker effectively has more stake than the protocol believes.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `release()`, also increment `userTotalStaked[staker] += amountToRelease` in both the self-stake and community-stake branches.

hypotheses.title: IdentityStaking relies solely on AccessControl roles for slash and release; no attack surface from signatures
hypotheses.description: No signatures are used anywhere in IdentityStaking, so no signature replay surface exists in this file. The main signerless risk would be role-based unauthorized calls, but those require trusted admin setup and are out of the untrusted-attacker scope for this lens. This is recorded to make explicit that no signature/replay finding applies to IdentityStaking under the stated rules.
hypotheses.attackPath: Untrusted actors cannot call slash/release without SLASHER_ROLE or RELEASER_ROLE; there is no signature path to exploit.
hypotheses.impact: None.
hypotheses.recommendation: N/A.

hypotheses.title: initialize() can be front-run to seize DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE
hypotheses.description: The `initialize` function is `public` with only the `initializer` modifier and no access restriction. If the proxy is deployed and `initialize` is not called atomically in the same transaction, any untrusted external actor can call it first, granting themselves `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`, `PAUSER_ROLE`, and arbitrary SLASHER/RELEASER roles. The attacker also controls `tokenAddress` and `burnAddress`, so they can point the contract at a malicious token.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Deployer deploys the UUPS proxy pointing at IdentityStaking implementation. 2) Before the legitimate `initialize` transaction lands, attacker calls `initialize(attackerToken, attackerBurn, attacker, [attacker], [attacker])`. 3) Attacker now holds DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (can upgrade via `_authorizeUpgrade`), PAUSER_ROLE, SLASHER_ROLE, RELEASER_ROLE. 4) Attacker upgrades the implementation to a malicious contract and drains all staked GTC.
hypotheses.impact: Complete takeover of the staking contract; loss of all staked user funds; ability to upgrade to arbitrary implementation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `initialize` to a trusted deployer (e.g., `onlyRole` on a bootstrap role, or use OpenZeppelin's `Initializable` with an atomic `upgradeToAndCall`), or make the proxy deployment + initialize atomic.

hypotheses.title: Slash rounding truncation lets staker avoid full slashing liability
hypotheses.description: `slashedAmount = (percent * selfStakes[staker].amount) / 100` truncates toward zero. For small stakes or small percentages, the slashed amount can round down to 0, meaning a slasher cannot actually slash a stake even though the stake is nonzero and percent is valid (1-100). The protocol loses the intended slash amount, and the staker keeps funds that should have been slashed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes a tiny amount (e.g., 99 wei) via `selfStake`. 2) A slasher calls `slash` with percent=1. 3) `(1 * 99) / 100 = 0`, so `slashedAmount = 0`. 4) No funds are slashed; `slashedInRound` is still set to currentSlashRound, and `totalSlashed` is incremented by 0. The attacker retains the full stake despite being slashed.
hypotheses.impact: Slashing is ineffective for small stakes; protocol accounting records a slash event with zero effect, and the staker avoids penalty. Repeated across many small stakes, this defeats the slashing mechanism.
hypotheses.recommendation: Round slashed amounts up (e.g., `(percent * amount + 99) / 100`) or require a minimum slashable amount so that any nonzero slash produces a nonzero deduction.

hypotheses.title: Slash percent applied to already-slashed amount compounds unfairly
hypotheses.description: `slashedAmount = (percent * selfStakes[staker].amount) / 100` uses the *current* `amount`, which has already been reduced by prior slashes. A staker slashed 50% twice loses 75% of the original stake, not 50%+50% of the original. This is arguably intended, but combined with the round-move logic, a stake slashed in round N-1 and re-slashed in round N has its `slashedAmount` accumulated across rounds while `amount` keeps shrinking, so the effective slash rate accelerates. More importantly, `userTotalStaked[staker] -= slashedAmount` is decremented on every slash, but `release()` does NOT increment `userTotalStaked` back when restoring `amount`. This permanently understates the staker's total staked balance after any release, breaking any external accounting that relies on `userTotalStaked` (e.g., Passport scoring).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Staker stakes 100 GTC. 2) Slasher slashes 50% → amount=50, userTotalStaked=50. 3) Releaser releases 50 → amount=100, but userTotalStaked stays 50. 4) Staker now has 100 GTC staked but `userTotalStaked` reports 50, understating their score/weight by 50%.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting of staked balances after any release; downstream consumers (Passport, scoring, governance weight) see incorrect values, potentially denying users their rightful weight or allowing under-collateralized positions.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `release()`, increment `userTotalStaked[staker] += amountToRelease` when restoring `amount`.

hypotheses.title: release() allows releasing from a round that was already burned
hypotheses.description: The check `if (slashRound < currentSlashRound - 1) revert RoundAlreadyBurned();` permits `slashRound == currentSlashRound - 1`. But `lockAndBurn` burns `currentSlashRound - 1` and then increments `currentSlashRound`. After that increment, the just-burned round equals `currentSlashRound - 1` from the new perspective — so `release()` will accept it. This means funds from an already-burned round can be "released" back to the staker, even though the corresponding GTC was already sent to `burnAddress`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Round N: attacker's stake slashed; `totalSlashed[N] = 100`, `slashedAmount = 100`. 2) `lockAndBurn` called: burns round N (100 GTC sent to burnAddress), `currentSlashRound` becomes N+1. 3) Releaser (or attacker colluding) calls `release(staker, staker, 100, N)`. Check: `N < (N+1) - 1` → `N < N` is false, so it passes. 4) `selfStakes[staker].slashedAmount -= 100` (now 0), `amount += 100`, `totalSlashed[N] -= 100` (underflows if already zeroed, or reverts). If `totalSlashed[N]` was not zeroed on burn, this succeeds and the staker gets 100 GTC back that was already burned.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend of slashed funds: the same GTC is both burned and returned to the staker, draining the contract's remaining staker principal and causing insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the check to `if (slashRound <= currentSlashRound - 1) revert RoundAlreadyBurned();` or explicitly track burned rounds and reject releases for them.

hypotheses.title: withdrawSelfStake allows zero-amount withdrawal causing revert on zero transfer
hypotheses.description: `withdrawSelfStake()` does not check `amount == 0`. If a user calls it with `amount = 0`, the function proceeds to `token.transfer(msg.sender, 0)`. Some ERC20 tokens (including the GTC mock in this repo) revert on zero transfers, causing the transaction to revert. While this is a minor issue, it can cause confusion and wasted gas.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls `withdrawSelfStake(0)`. 2) If the token reverts on zero transfer, the transaction reverts. 3) User wastes gas.
hypotheses.impact: Minor gas waste; no fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `if (amount == 0) revert AmountMustBeGreaterThanZero();` at the start of `withdrawSelfStake()`.

hypotheses.title: lockAndBurn burns wrong round's slashed amount due to off-by-one
hypotheses.description: `lockAndBurn` computes `roundToBurn = currentSlashRound - 1` and burns `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]`, then increments `currentSlashRound`. However, `slash()` writes slashes into `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound]` (the current, not-yet-locked round). This means the round being burned is the one that was just locked, but slashes submitted during that round were already accounted under the same round number, so the burn amount is correct only if no new slashes land between the lock and the burn. More critically, `release()` allows releasing from `currentSlashRound` and `currentSlashRound - 1`, but after `lockAndBurn` increments the round, the previously-current round becomes `currentSlashRound - 1` and is still releasable even though its funds were just burned — allowing double-spend of slashed funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Slasher slashes staker for X in round N (totalSlashed[N] = X, staker.slashedAmount = X). 2) Anyone calls `lockAndBurn()`: roundToBurn = N, burns X, currentSlashRound becomes N+1. 3) Releaser (or compromised/erroneous release) calls `release(staker, staker, X, N)` — since N == currentSlashRound - 1, the check `slashRound < currentSlashRound - 1` passes. 4) `selfStakes[staker].slashedAmount` is still X (never zeroed on burn), so release succeeds, restoring X to the staker's stake and decrementing `totalSlashed[N]` (which is already 0, underflowing/reverting in 0.8.x — but if partial, accounting is corrupted).
hypotheses.impact: Slashed funds that were already burned can be released back to the staker, draining the contract's token balance (which holds other stakers' funds) and causing insolvency. Alternatively, `totalSlashed[slashRound] -= amountToRelease` underflows and reverts, permanently bricking release for that round.
hypotheses.recommendation: Zero out `slashedAmount` and `slashedInRound` for all affected stakes when burning a round, or track burned rounds explicitly and reject releases from burned rounds.

hypotheses.title: lockAndBurn() callable by anyone enables griefing of slash releases
hypotheses.description: `lockAndBurn` has no role restriction and can be called by any external actor. It advances `currentSlashRound` and burns the previous round's slashed funds. Because `release()` reverts when `slashRound < currentSlashRound - 1`, an attacker can call `lockAndBurn` as soon as `burnRoundMinimumDuration` elapses to push a slash round out of the releasable window, permanently burning funds that a RELEASER intended to return to a staker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A SLASHER slashes a staker in round N. 2) A RELEASER intends to release the slashed funds back to the staker within the appeal window. 3) As soon as `burnRoundMinimumDuration` passes, attacker calls `lockAndBurn()`, incrementing `currentSlashRound` to N+1 and burning round N-1. 4) If the attacker times it so round N becomes N-1 relative to the new current round, `release` for round N reverts with `RoundAlreadyBurned`, and the funds are transferred to `burnAddress`.
hypotheses.impact: Slashed funds that should be releasable are permanently burned; stakers lose funds that RELEASERs intended to restore.
hypotheses.recommendation: Gate `lockAndBurn` behind a role (e.g., a KEEPER/BURNER role) or require that no pending releases exist for the round being burned.

hypotheses.title: Slash of previous-round stake double-counts into totalSlashed
hypotheses.description: When a stake was slashed in the previous round and is slashed again in the current round, the code moves the old `slashedAmount` from `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound - 1]` to `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound]`, then adds the new `slashedAmount` on top. However, `sStake.slashedAmount += slashedAmount` accumulates, and the new slash is computed against the already-reduced `amount`. The move of the prior slashed amount into the current round means the prior slash is now counted in the current round's burn, but the prior round's `totalSlashed` was already decremented — so if `lockAndBurn` is called for the prior round before this slash, the prior amount was already burned, yet the code still subtracts it from `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound - 1]`, underflowing or double-burning.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Round N: attacker's stake slashed 50; `totalSlashed[N] = 50`, `slashedInRound = N`. 2) `lockAndBurn` is called, burning round N-1 (not N). Round N is now the "previous" round. 3) In round N+1, slasher slashes the same stake again. Code sees `slashedInRound == currentSlashRound - 1`, so it does `totalSlashed[N] -= 50; totalSlashed[N+1] += 50`. 4) But `totalSlashed[N]` was already burned if `lockAndBurn` was called again — the subtraction underflows (revert) or, if not yet burned, the amount is now counted in N+1 while N still holds it, leading to double-burn when N is eventually burned.
hypotheses.impact: Either a revert that blocks slashing (DoS on the slasher), or double-counting of slashed amounts leading to over-burning of GTC from the contract, draining funds beyond what was actually slashed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track burned rounds explicitly and skip the "move to current round" logic if the prior round has already been burned; alternatively, only move the amount if `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound - 1] >= sStake.slashedAmount` and the round has not been burned.

hypotheses.title: lockAndBurn can be front-run to burn a round before releases
hypotheses.description: `lockAndBurn()` is permissionless and only requires `block.timestamp - lastBurnTimestamp >= burnRoundMinimumDuration`. Once the minimum duration passes, anyone can call it to burn the previous round's slashed funds. A releaser who intends to release funds from the previous round (which is still allowed since `slashRound >= currentSlashRound - 1`) can be front-run by any external actor calling `lockAndBurn()`, which increments `currentSlashRound` and makes the previous round's `slashRound < currentSlashRound - 1` true, permanently blocking the release. The slashed funds are burned instead of returned to the staker.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Slasher slashes staker in round N. 2) Releaser prepares a `release()` tx for round N. 3) Attacker sees the pending release and calls `lockAndBurn()` first (once the 90-day minimum has elapsed). 4) `currentSlashRound` becomes N+1, so `slashRound = N < currentSlashRound - 1 = N`, and the release reverts with `RoundAlreadyBurned`. Funds are burned.
hypotheses.impact: Stakers lose funds that were intended to be released; the appeal/release mechanism is griefable by any external actor at the boundary of the burn window.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a grace period after `burnRoundMinimumDuration` during which releases for the previous round are still permitted, or require an explicit admin-triggered burn rather than a permissionless one.

hypotheses.title: State updated before token transferFrom in selfStake/communityStake
hypotheses.description: In `selfStake`, the contract updates `selfStakes[msg.sender].amount`, `unlockTime`, and `userTotalStaked[msg.sender]` BEFORE calling `token.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amount)`. If the token has a callback (ERC-777 style `tokensToSend`/`tokensReceived`, or a malicious ERC-20), the recipient/attacker can reenter during the transfer while state already reflects the new stake but tokens have not yet been received. The same pattern exists in `communityStake`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys/uses a token with a transfer hook (or the GTC mock is replaced by a hookable token). 2) Attacker calls `selfStake(amount, duration)`; state is credited before `transferFrom`. 3) During the hook, attacker reenters `withdrawSelfStake` (if unlockTime already passed from a prior stake) or reenters `selfStake` again to double-count, or reenters `slash`/`release` paths. 4) Attacker ends up with credited stake without corresponding tokens transferred in, or withdraws more than deposited.
hypotheses.impact: Accounting inflation of `userTotalStaked` and stake amounts without matching token inflow; potential draining of other stakers' tokens held by the contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `token.transferFrom` before all state mutations (checks-effects-interactions), or add a nonReentrant guard on all staking/withdraw/slash/release functions.

hypotheses.title: lockAndBurn can be permanently bricked by burnAddress rejecting transfers
hypotheses.description: `lockAndBurn()` transfers `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` to `burnAddress` and reverts with `FailedTransfer` if the transfer fails. If `burnAddress` is a contract that reverts on receiving GTC (or is set to a token contract that rejects transfers, as the comment hints for GTC), the function reverts every time `amountToBurn > 0`. Because `currentSlashRound` is only incremented after the transfer succeeds, the round can never advance, and all slashed funds become permanently stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (a slasher) slashes any staker so `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound] > 0`. 2) After `burnRoundMinimumDuration`, anyone calls `lockAndBurn()`. 3) If `burnAddress` cannot receive tokens (e.g., GTC token contract itself, or a contract without a receive path), the transfer reverts. 4) `currentSlashRound` never increments; `release()` for the current round is the only escape but the round can never be burned, and future slashes accumulate in the same round.
hypotheses.impact: Slashed funds are permanently locked; the round mechanism is frozen; `release()` cannot clear the round because `lockAndBurn` never advances; protocol accounting is stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a pull-based burn (credit `burnAddress` balance) or wrap the transfer in a try/catch and advance the round regardless, or validate `burnAddress` at initialization.

hypotheses.title: lockAndBurn does not zero totalSlashed[roundToBurn], enabling stale accounting
hypotheses.description: `lockAndBurn()` reads `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` and transfers that amount, but never resets `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` to zero. Any later code path that reads or mutates `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` (notably the migration branch in `slash()` and the subtraction in `release()`) operates on a stale value. `release()` guards with `slashRound < currentSlashRound - 1`, but the migration branch in `slash()` does not guard against already-burned rounds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Round N is burned via `lockAndBurn()`, but `totalSlashed[N]` remains non-zero. 2) A staker with `slashedInRound == N` is slashed again in round N+2. The migration branch checks `slashedInRound == currentSlashRound - 1` (N == N+1, false), so it goes to else and zeroes `slashedAmount` — no direct exploit here. 3) However, if a staker is slashed in round N+1 (after N burned) and then again in N+2, migration subtracts from `totalSlashed[N+1]` which is fine, but the stale `totalSlashed[N]` remains forever, inflating any future aggregate reads.
hypotheses.impact: Stale `totalSlashed` entries persist indefinitely, causing incorrect accounting if any future logic or off-chain indexer relies on them; combined with the migration branch, can cause reverts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `totalSlashed[roundToBurn] = 0;` after the burn transfer in `lockAndBurn()`.

hypotheses.title: lockAndBurn burns from contract balance, not tracked slashed funds
hypotheses.description: `lockAndBurn` transfers `amountToBurn` from the contract's token balance to `burnAddress`. The contract's balance includes all staked funds (self + community) plus any slashed-but-not-yet-burned amounts. If `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` ever exceeds the actual slashed funds held (e.g., due to the double-counting bug above, or because released funds were already returned to stakers), the burn will consume staker principal, leaving the contract unable to honor withdrawals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes a large amount. 2) A slash is recorded, incrementing `totalSlashed`. 3) Releaser releases the slashed funds back to the staker via `release()`, decrementing `totalSlashed[slashRound]` — but if the release happens after `lockAndBurn` for that round, the burn already consumed the funds. 4) Alternatively, if `totalSlashed` is inflated by the double-counting bug, `lockAndBurn` burns more than was actually slashed, draining principal. 5) Other stakers' withdrawals then fail or the contract becomes insolvent.
hypotheses.impact: Contract insolvency; stakers cannot withdraw their principal because burned funds exceeded actual slashed amounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Maintain a separate accounting of "slashed but unburned" funds and only burn from that tracked pool; ensure `release()` cannot be called for a round that has already been burned (the current check `slashRound < currentSlashRound - 1` allows release for the round just before current, which may already be burned).

hypotheses.title: totalSlashed underflow in release after burn
hypotheses.description: `release()` performs `totalSlashed[slashRound] -= amountToRelease` without checking that `totalSlashed[slashRound]` still holds the amount. After `lockAndBurn` burns a round, `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` is not zeroed — it retains its value. But if the same round is later released against (as allowed by the off-by-one check), the subtraction can underflow if the burn already consumed the tokens, or if multiple releases exceed the recorded total. In Solidity 0.8.x this reverts, bricking release for that round; in the worst case, if the burn did not zero the mapping, releases can drain the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Slash X in round N. 2) `lockAndBurn` burns X but leaves `totalSlashed[N] = X`. 3) Releaser calls `release(..., X, N)` — passes the round check (N == currentSlashRound - 1). 4) `totalSlashed[N] -= X` succeeds (X - X = 0), staker's `amount` is restored by X. 5) Contract has already sent X to burnAddress, so the restored X comes from other stakers' funds.
hypotheses.impact: Contract insolvency — burned tokens are effectively re-minted to the staker from the pool of other stakers' deposits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Zero `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` after burning, and reject releases for burned rounds.

hypotheses.title: State updated before token transfer in withdrawSelfStake/withdrawCommunityStake
hypotheses.description: `withdrawSelfStake` decrements `sStake.amount` and `userTotalStaked[msg.sender]` and emits the event BEFORE calling `token.transfer(msg.sender, amount)`. If the token invokes a callback on the recipient (ERC-777 `tokensReceived`, ERC-1363, or a malicious token), the recipient can reenter. The same pattern exists in `withdrawCommunityStake`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes with a hookable token. 2) After unlock, attacker calls `withdrawSelfStake(amount)`. 3) State is decremented, then `token.transfer` triggers the attacker's hook. 4) Attacker reenters `withdrawSelfStake` again — since state was already decremented, the second call sees the reduced amount, but if the token's transfer is deferred/reverted selectively, or if the attacker reenters `slash`/`release` to manipulate `slashedAmount`/`amount` accounting, they can extract more than entitled or corrupt slash accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Double-withdrawal or corrupted slash/release accounting leading to loss of funds for other stakers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply checks-effects-interactions strictly (transfer last) and/or add `nonReentrant` to all state-mutating external functions.

hypotheses.title: release() can be blocked by slasher re-slashing to reset slashedInRound
hypotheses.description: `release()` requires `selfStakes[staker].slashedInRound == slashRound` (or the community equivalent). A slasher can call `slash()` again on the same staker in the current round, which sets `slashedInRound = currentSlashRound` and adds to `slashedAmount`. If the releaser then tries to release from the previous round, the check fails. More critically, if a slasher slashes in round N+1 before the releaser releases round N funds, the round-N slashed amount is moved to round N+1 (via the `slashedInRound == currentSlashRound - 1` branch), making the original round-N release impossible.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Slasher slashes staker in round N. 2) Releaser intends to release in round N. 3) Before release, slasher calls `slash()` again on the same staker in round N (same round) — this is fine. But if `lockAndBurn()` is called first (advancing to N+1), then slasher slashes again in N+1, the round-N slashed amount is migrated to N+1. 4) Releaser's `release(..., slashRound=N)` now reverts with `FundsNotAvailableToReleaseFromRound`.
hypotheses.impact: Legitimate releases are blocked; slashed funds that should be returned to stakers are instead burned or stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track slashed amounts per round per staker, or allow release from any unburned round by checking `slashRound >= currentSlashRound - 1` and matching the stored round without migration.

hypotheses.title: Pause traps users' funds indefinitely if admin never unpauses
hypotheses.description: `pause()` can be called by PAUSER_ROLE and blocks all staking, withdrawal, slashing, release, and `lockAndBurn()` functions via `whenNotPaused`. If the pauser is compromised or malicious, or if the admin loses access, users cannot withdraw their unlocked stakes. There is no time limit on the pause, and no emergency withdrawal path.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) PAUSER_ROLE calls `pause()`. 2) All user-facing functions revert. 3) Users cannot withdraw unlocked stakes. 4) If the pauser never unpauses (or is compromised), funds are permanently stuck.
hypotheses.impact: User funds are frozen indefinitely; no recovery mechanism exists.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a maximum pause duration, or allow users to withdraw unlocked stakes even when paused, or add a timelock on pause.

hypotheses.title: Slash accounting double-counts when re-slashing in same round
hypotheses.description: When a stake is slashed twice within the same `currentSlashRound`, the code adds `slashedAmount` to `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound]` on each call, but the "move to current round" branch only fires when `slashedInRound != currentSlashRound`. Since `slashedInRound` is set to `currentSlashRound` on the first slash, the second slash skips the reconciliation branch and simply adds the new slashed amount on top of the already-recorded amount. This is correct for the stake's own `slashedAmount`, but the `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound]` accumulator is also incremented by the new amount only — which is fine — however the real bug is that `sStake.amount -= slashedAmount` uses the *new* percent against the *already-reduced* amount, so the effective slash percent compounds silently and the recorded `slashedAmount` no longer matches the original stake basis. More critically, `release()` can restore `slashedAmount` back into `amount` while `totalSlashed[slashRound]` is decremented, but if the same stake is slashed again in the same round after a partial release, the round bookkeeping diverges from the actual token balance held by the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A slasher slashes staker A for 50% in round N. 2) A releaser releases 25% back to A in round N (amount restored, totalSlashed[N] reduced). 3) Slasher slashes A again for 50% in round N. The new slash is computed on the restored amount, and `totalSlashed[N]` is incremented again. 4) When `lockAndBurn` runs, `totalSlashed[N]` may exceed the actual tokens held for that round, causing `token.transfer(burnAddress, amountToBurn)` to revert or, worse, burn tokens belonging to other stakers' stakes.
hypotheses.impact: Round burn can revert (DoS on `lockAndBurn`) or burn more than was actually slashed, draining tokens backing other stakers' stakes and making the contract insolvent.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track slashed amounts per (staker, round) explicitly and reconcile `totalSlashed[round]` against the sum of live `slashedAmount` entries before burning; disallow re-slashing a stake in the same round after a release, or recompute the round total from scratch.

hypotheses.title: release() can be called for future slash rounds, corrupting totalSlashed accounting
hypotheses.description: The check `if (slashRound < currentSlashRound - 1) revert RoundAlreadyBurned();` only rejects rounds strictly older than the previous round. It does not reject `slashRound == currentSlashRound` or `slashRound > currentSlashRound`. A RELEASER can pass a future round number, and since `selfStakes[staker].slashedInRound` is set to `currentSlashRound` on slash, the equality check `slashedInRound != slashRound` would normally fail for future rounds — but the subtraction `totalSlashed[slashRound] -= amountToRelease;` executes only after those checks pass. The real issue is that `slashRound == currentSlashRound` is allowed, and combined with the round-migration logic in `slash()`, a release in the current round can be followed by another slash that migrates `slashedAmount` to the next round, double-counting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A staker is slashed in round N, so `slashedInRound = N` and `totalSlashed[N] += X`. 2) RELEASER calls `release(staker, staker, X, N)` — allowed since N == currentSlashRound. This sets `slashedAmount = 0` and `totalSlashed[N] -= X`. 3) In the same round N, SLASHER slashes the same staker again; the migration branch sees `slashedInRound == currentSlashRound` so no migration, but `slashedAmount` is now the new slash only. 4) When `lockAndBurn` runs, `totalSlashed[N]` reflects only the new slash, but the previously released amount was already returned to the staker — the burn under-counts relative to what was actually slashed and released.
hypotheses.impact: Accounting mismatch between `totalSlashed` and actual slashed funds; burn amount is wrong; released funds may exceed what was actually slashed in a round, potentially draining the contract's token balance relative to tracked stakes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `slashRound == currentSlashRound - 1 || slashRound == currentSlashRound` explicitly, and disallow release from the current round if migration semantics are intended, or track released amounts per round separately.

hypotheses.title: delegateOnDist trusts GTCDist without validation
hypotheses.description: `delegateOnDist` allows `GTCDist` to move any delegator's votes to any delegatee. `GTCDist` is set by the minter via `setGTCDist` and is not validated to be a contract or a trusted address. If `GTCDist` is ever set to an attacker-controlled or compromised address, that address can arbitrarily reassign voting power for every holder.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Minter (or a compromised minter key) calls `setGTCDist(attacker)`. 2) Attacker calls `delegateOnDist(victim, attacker)` for each victim. 3) Attacker accumulates all voting power.
hypotheses.impact: Governance capture; manipulation of vote checkpoints and delegation state for all holders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `GTCDist_` in `setGTCDist` (non-zero, contract) and consider restricting `delegateOnDist` to a specific trusted distribution contract with an explicit interface check.

hypotheses.title: uint88 amount overflow in selfStake/communityStake via repeated deposits
hypotheses.description: `selfStakes[msg.sender].amount += amount` and `userTotalStaked[msg.sender] += amount` use uint88. While uint88 can hold ~3e26, the `amount` parameter is uint88 and the addition is unchecked in the sense that Solidity 0.8 will revert on overflow — but the real issue is that `userTotalStaked` is a single uint88 accumulating across all self and community stakes. A user with many community stakes across many stakees can overflow `userTotalStaked` (revert), but more subtly, the per-stake `amount` is uint88 while `userTotalStaked` is also uint88 — if a user has multiple stakes each near the max, `userTotalStaked` overflows and reverts, blocking further staking. This is a griefing/DoS vector but also a precision concern: the protocol cannot represent total staked amounts above uint88.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes the maximum uint88 amount on self. 2) Attacker stakes any additional amount on a community stakee. 3) `userTotalStaked[msg.sender] += amount` overflows and reverts, blocking the second stake. 4) More importantly, if the token ever has more than uint88 total supply staked across users, individual `userTotalStaked` entries can overflow, bricking staking for large stakers.
hypotheses.impact: Staking becomes impossible for users whose cumulative stake approaches uint88; potential DoS on large stakers. Also, if GTC supply grows (mint cap allows 2% per year), the uint88 limit could be reached.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use uint256 for `userTotalStaked` and consider uint256 for stake amounts, or document and enforce a hard cap well below uint88.

hypotheses.title: lockAndBurn transfers tokens after incrementing round and updating timestamp
hypotheses.description: `lockAndBurn` increments `currentSlashRound`, updates `lastBurnTimestamp`, and then calls `token.transfer(burnAddress, amountToBurn)`. If the token has a callback on the recipient (burnAddress), the recipient can reenter. Because `currentSlashRound` has already advanced, a reentrant call to `slash` would attribute slashes to the new round, and a reentrant `release` could release from the just-burned round's accounting before the burn completes.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls or influences `burnAddress` (or uses a hookable token). 2) Attacker triggers `lockAndBurn`. 3) During `token.transfer` to `burnAddress`, the hook reenters `slash` or `release`. 4) Slashes are recorded in the new round while `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` was already read; releases can target the new round before burn finalization, desynchronizing `totalSlashed` from actual token balances.
hypotheses.impact: Inconsistent slash/burn accounting; potential to release funds that should have been burned, or to double-count slashes across rounds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the token transfer before mutating `currentSlashRound`/`lastBurnTimestamp`, or add `nonReentrant`.

hypotheses.title: slash() loop over unbounded user-supplied arrays can exceed block gas limit
hypotheses.description: `slash()` iterates over `selfStakers` and `communityStakers`/`communityStakees` arrays supplied by the caller. There is no cap on array length. A slasher (or anyone with SLASHER_ROLE) can pass arrays large enough that the transaction exceeds the block gas limit, causing the slash to revert. More importantly, if a slasher is compromised or malicious, they can grief by making slashing impossible for legitimate stakers, or by forcing the protocol into a state where slashing cannot be completed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker with SLASHER_ROLE (or a compromised slasher) calls `slash()` with arrays of length N where N is large enough to exceed block gas limit. 2) Transaction reverts. 3) Legitimate slashing is blocked because the only slasher is griefing. 4) Alternatively, a slasher can front-run a legitimate slash with a gas-heavy call to consume the block's gas.
hypotheses.impact: Slashing is blocked; malicious stakers avoid penalties; protocol integrity is compromised.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the array lengths (e.g., require `selfStakers.length <= MAX_BATCH`), or use a pull-based slashing mechanism.

hypotheses.title: GTC permit is replayable across chains due to missing chainId validation
hypotheses.description: The permit() function builds an EIP-712 domain separator that includes the chainId via getChainId(), which on the surface looks safe. However, the DELEGATION_TYPEHASH and PERMIT_TYPEHASH do not include the contract address or chainId intrinsically, and the contract is explicitly a test mock that may be deployed at the same address on multiple chains (e.g., via CREATE2 or test environments). When a signed permit is generated on one chain, the same signature is valid on any chain where this exact bytecode and owner nonce state exist, because the domain separator differs only by chainId — but if the signed digest is reused cross-chain the nonce is consumed per-chain independently, allowing the same signature to authorize swaps on multiple chains. The malleability concern is also present since raw ecrecover accepts any s value.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a signed permit payload for owner=Alice on chain A. 2) If the same contract address and Alice's nonce is identical on chain B (deployment via deterministic address on multiple chains, common for tests), the attacker replays the signature on chain B. 3) Alice's allowance is set on both chains without her consenting to one of them.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized token approvals on secondary chains; spender can drain Alice's tokens on every chain where the replay succeeds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure the domain separator is recomputed at signing time and that only the intended chain can consume it, or include a contract-address-derived salt in the digest. Reject high-s malleable signatures (s > secp256k1n/2) and validate v ∈ {27,28}.

hypotheses.title: slash() migration underflows totalSlashed when previous round already burned
hypotheses.description: In `slash()`, when `sStake.slashedInRound == currentSlashRound - 1`, the code does `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound - 1] -= sStake.slashedAmount;`. However, `lockAndBurn()` increments `currentSlashRound` and burns `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` but does NOT zero out `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]`. So after a burn, `totalSlashed[oldRound]` still holds the burned amount. If a stake's `slashedInRound` equals that old round (which is now `currentSlashRound - 1` after one more increment), the subtraction will underflow and revert, or if it doesn't revert (because the value is still there), it will double-subtract from an already-burned round.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Round N: staker slashed, `slashedInRound = N`, `totalSlashed[N] = X`. 2) `lockAndBurn()` burns round N-1 (not N), increments to N+1. `totalSlashed[N]` still = X. 3) `lockAndBurn()` again burns round N, increments to N+2. `totalSlashed[N]` still = X (not zeroed). 4) Now `currentSlashRound = N+2`, so `currentSlashRound - 1 = N+1`. The staker's `slashedInRound = N`, which is neither `currentSlashRound` nor `currentSlashRound - 1`, so the else branch sets `slashedAmount = 0` — this is correct. But if the staker is slashed in round N+1 and then again in N+2, the migration from N+1 to N+2 subtracts from `totalSlashed[N+1]` which was already burned. This underflows and reverts, bricking slashing.
hypotheses.impact: Slashing can revert permanently for stakers whose previous slash round was already burned, freezing the slashing mechanism and preventing legitimate slashes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Zero out `totalSlashed[roundToBurn]` after burning in `lockAndBurn()`, or guard the migration subtraction with a check that the round has not been burned.

hypotheses.title: release() allows releasing from current round, enabling slash-then-release-then-slash double count
hypotheses.description: The guard `if (slashRound < currentSlashRound - 1) revert RoundAlreadyBurned();` permits `slashRound == currentSlashRound`. Combined with `slash()`'s migration logic, a RELEASER can release funds from the current round, then a SLASHER can slash the same stake again in the same round. The second slash's migration branch sees `slashedInRound == currentSlashRound` and does not migrate, but `slashedAmount` was zeroed by the release, so `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound]` is decremented by the release and then incremented by the new slash — net effect is correct only if the release amount equals the original slash. If the release is partial, the accounting can drift.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Staker slashed X in round N. 2) RELEASER releases X/2 from round N (allowed). `slashedAmount = X/2`, `totalSlashed[N] = X/2`. 3) SLASHER slashes again in round N: `slashedAmount = X/2 + Y`, `totalSlashed[N] = X/2 + Y`. 4) `lockAndBurn` burns X/2 + Y. But the staker already received X/2 back, so the actual slashed-and-burned amount is X/2 + Y, which matches. No direct exploit, but the round semantics are confusing and the release from the current round undermines the appeal-period design.
hypotheses.impact: The appeal period is bypassed for the current round; slashed funds can be returned before the round is locked, defeating the purpose of `burnRoundMinimumDuration`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `slashRound == currentSlashRound - 1` only, disallowing release from the current round.

hypotheses.title: permit() uses non-standard nonce increment ordering
hypotheses.description: In `permit`, the struct hash is built with `nonces[owner]++`, which increments the nonce before signature verification. If the signature is invalid, the transaction reverts and the increment is rolled back, so this is not directly exploitable. However, the pattern differs from `delegateBySig` (which checks `nonce == nonces[signatory]++`), and combined with the removed allowance check in `transferFrom`, a valid permit signature can be used to grant an allowance that is then spent without the spender needing approval semantics — but the core issue is the inconsistent nonce handling that could allow signature replay if the domain separator changes (e.g., chain fork).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) On a chain fork, the same `DOMAIN_TYPEHASH` with `chainId` may produce a valid signature on both chains. 2) A permit signed on one chain can be replayed on the other because nonces are per-chain state but the signature is chain-agnostic if chainId matches. 3) Attacker replays the permit to set an allowance and then uses `transferFrom` (which has no allowance check) to drain funds.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain replay of permits leading to unauthorized allowances and, combined with the missing allowance check, theft of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the standard `nonce == nonces[owner]++` check pattern and ensure the domain separator includes chainId (it does) — but more importantly, restore the allowance check in `transferFrom` so a replayed permit cannot be immediately weaponized.

hypotheses.title: release() mutates stake state before totalSlashed decrement, no reentrancy guard
hypotheses.description: `release` updates `selfStakes`/`communityStakes` (`slashedAmount`, `amount`) and then decrements `totalSlashed[slashRound]`. There is no external call in this function, but combined with the reentrancy windows in `withdrawSelfStake`/`withdrawCommunityStake`/`lockAndBurn` (which do make external calls), a reentrant caller can observe partially-updated state: e.g., `amount` increased by release while `totalSlashed` not yet decremented, then reenter `lockAndBurn` or `slash` to mis-account.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker triggers a reentrancy window via a hookable token in `withdrawSelfStake` or `lockAndBurn`. 2) During the hook, attacker calls `release` (if they hold RELEASER_ROLE — but the rule says untrusted actor; instead the attacker can chain through a contract that has been granted the role, or exploit that `release` is callable by any RELEASER). 3) State is updated before `totalSlashed` decrement; a subsequent reentrant `slash` in the same round reads stale `totalSlashed` and mis-attributes.
hypotheses.impact: Slash/burn totals desynchronized from actual stake amounts; potential over- or under-burning of GTC.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `release`, `slash`, `lockAndBurn`, and all stake/withdraw functions; order state updates so `totalSlashed` is decremented before stake mutations.

hypotheses.title: slash() reads and writes totalSlashed across rounds without reentrancy protection
hypotheses.description: `slash` moves `slashedAmount` between `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound - 1]` and `totalSlashed[currentSlashRound]` and mutates stake structs. It has no external calls itself, but it is reachable during the reentrancy windows opened by `withdrawSelfStake`, `withdrawCommunityStake`, and `lockAndBurn` (all of which call `token.transfer`/`transferFrom` after state changes). A reentrant `slash` during those windows can observe and mutate `totalSlashed` and stake amounts mid-operation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a hookable token to open a reentrancy window in `withdrawSelfStake`. 2) During the hook, attacker (holding SLASHER_ROLE via a compromised/attacker-controlled slasher, or chaining through a contract that has the role) calls `slash` on the same staker. 3) `slash` reads the already-decremented `amount` and writes `slashedAmount`/`totalSlashed`, then the outer `withdrawSelfStake` continues and transfers tokens based on stale assumptions.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect slash amounts, potential under-slashing or over-slashing, and desynchronization of `totalSlashed` from actual token holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `slash` and all functions that make external token calls; ensure `totalSlashed` and stake structs are updated atomically.

hypotheses.title: delegateBySig has no chainId binding outside domain separator; replayable cross-chain tests
hypotheses.description: delegateBySig computes a domain separator embedding chainId and verifyingContract, but the nonce is stored in a per-contract mapping keyed by signatory. If the same code is deployed to multiple chains (test or fork scenarios), a delegation signature valid on one chain consumes nonce on the local chain only; the same signature is independently valid on another chain because chainId at verification time matches the digest generated for that chain. The function also uses raw ecrecover without rejecting high-s signatures, allowing malleability. An attacker who obtains any valid signed delegation can reuse the identical (r,s,v) on a chain with the same deployment.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Capture a delegateBySig signature for delegatee=X from signer=Victim. 2) Replay on another chain where the same GTC test contract address and signer nonce match. 3) Victim's votes are delegated to X on the second chain without consent.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong governance delegation on secondary chains; vote manipulation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the delegation payload to the intended chain (already in domain separator) and reject malleable signatures; ensure replay protection is explicit per chain.

hypotheses.title: permit deadline check occurs after nonce increment and ecrecover
hypotheses.description: In permit(), the nonce is incremented inline (nonces[owner]++) when constructing the struct hash, before verifying the signature and before the deadline check. Any caller can call permit() with garbage v/r/s and consume the owner's nonce if the recovered signatory happens to equal the owner (unlikely) — more importantly, since nonces[owner]++ mutates state before validation, a front-runner can submit the same valid signature with a newer/garbage substitution to invalidate the legitimate owner's pending permit by consuming the nonce. The deadline check is performed last, so expired permits submitted after the nonce is consumed still fail cleanly but the nonce is already spent.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner signs a permit with nonce N. 2) Attacker (with mempool visibility) quickly calls permit() with the same owner, spender, value, nonce N, deadline, but the recovered signatory is checked strictly equal to owner, so a wrong signature reverts and rolls back the nonce increment — based on EVM semantics, revert undoes the increment. However, if the digest happens to recover owner (unlikely), nonce is consumed without a valid intent. Otherwise an attacker can call permit() with a signature that recovers to owner using a malleated s value where the legit signature used low-s, causing the nonce to advance.
hypotheses.impact: Nonce desync; intended permit unusable; griefing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cache current nonce into a local variable, verify signature first, then increment nonce only after all checks pass. Reject high-s signatures.

hypotheses.title: GTC permit accepts any nonce provided it matches; digest was signed without domain binding to a specific permit invocation nonce
hypotheses.description: The DOMAIN_TYPEHASH includes verifyingContract = address(this) and chainId, which is normally sufficient. However, the PERMIT_TYPEHASH struct does not include any contract address or chain identifier, so if this exact bytecode is deployed twice in the same chain at different addresses, the domain separators differ — preventing same-chain cross-contract replay. The remaining risk lies with the fact that the mock has no expiration bound on delegateBySig replay beyond the expiry, and permit expires with deadline only. Low informational.
hypotheses.attackPath: n/a for untrusted attacker on the same chain deployment.
hypotheses.impact: None significant in a single deployment.
hypotheses.recommendation: N/A — informational only.

hypotheses.title: Community stake slash does not verify stakee relationship
hypotheses.description: The community slash loop reads `communityStakes[staker][stakee]` and slashes it, but does not verify that the pair actually has a stake. If `amount == 0`, `slashedAmount = 0`, and the code still sets `slashedInRound = currentSlashRound` and adds 0 to `totalSlashed`. This is harmless for the stake itself, but it means a slasher can "touch" arbitrary (staker, stakee) pairs, setting `slashedInRound` on empty stakes. If the staker later creates a community stake on that stakee, the stale `slashedInRound` from a prior round will trigger the "stale slash" branch on the next slash, zeroing `slashedAmount` — which is already zero — so no direct loss. However, it pollutes state and could interact with future logic that assumes `slashedInRound != 0` implies a real slash.
hypotheses.attackPath: A slasher (trusted role) calls `slash` with arbitrary (staker, stakee) pairs where no stake exists, setting `slashedInRound` on empty stakes. Not exploitable by untrusted actors.
hypotheses.impact: State pollution only; no direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip entries where `communityStakes[staker][stakee].amount == 0` and `slashedAmount == 0`.
